label: Malki et al. (2024)
authors: L. M. Malki, I. Kaleva, D. Patel, M. Warner, R. Abu-Salma
title: Exploring Privacy Practices of Female mHealth Apps in a Post-Roe World
venue: Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
use: Closest end-to-end comparator: app screening, policy/Data Safety analysis, hybrid cognitive walkthrough and heuristic inspection, codebook iteration and cross-surface triangulation. Read Methods §§3.1–3.4 and appendices.
caution: Its UK/US Android sample and recent-review ranking are precedents to compare, not rules for Germany; its iterative team coding is not automatically your independent two-coder reliability design.

label: Hutton et al. (2018)
authors: L. Hutton, B. A. Price, R. Kelly, C. McCormick, A. K. Bandara, T. Hatzakis, M. Meadows, B. Nuseibeh
title: Assessing the Privacy of mHealth Apps for Self-Tracking: Heuristic Evaluation Approach
use: Privacy-focused heuristic assessment of self-tracking apps: use its privacy dimensions and evaluation instrument to draft observable checklist items and evidence fields.
caution: Heuristic privacy appraisal is not a user cognitive walkthrough; neither proves deployed security or actual harms.

label: Shipp & Blasco (2020)
authors: L. Shipp, J. Blasco
title: How private is your period?: A systematic analysis of menstrual app privacy policies
use: Direct policy-analysis comparator for menstrual tracking: extract policy acquisition, coding categories, data types/recipients, and reporting of absent or incomplete disclosures.
caution: Policy statements describe communication; they do not by themselves establish actual app behaviour.

label: Alfawzan et al. (2022)
authors: N. Alfawzan, M. Christen, G. Spitale, N. Biller-Andorno
title: Privacy, Data Sharing, and Data Security Policies of Women’s mHealth Apps: Scoping Review and Content Analysis
use: App-review screening flow, keyword development, rating/download cutoff reasoning, access exclusions, policy assessment and independent assessment by two reviewers.
caution: Published thresholds and category-specific cutoffs belong to that corpus. The latest meeting rejects fixed category quotas; compare the rationale, not the numbers.

label: O'Loughlin et al. (2019)
authors: K. O'Loughlin, M. Neary, E. C. Adkins, S. M. Schueller
title: Reviewing the data security and privacy policies of mobile apps for depression
when: A/D/C; mental-health inclusion and missing policies
use: Depression-app review focused on transparency of security and privacy policies; useful for recording policy absence, disclosed practices and app-level characteristics.
caution: Transparency of a described safeguard is different from testing its implementation; adapt historical market and app-selection rules.

label: Robillard et al. (2019)
authors: J. M. Robillard, T. L. Feng, A. B. Sporn, J. A. Lai, C. Lo, M. Ta, R. Nadler
title: Availability, readability, and content of privacy policies and terms of agreements of mental health apps
use: Mental-health policy availability, readability and content: helps broaden beyond fertility and retain apps without policies as an explicit outcome.
caution: English-language policy analysis does not transfer its readability metrics or prevalence estimates automatically to German text.

label: Sunyaev et al. (2015)
authors: A. Sunyaev, T. Dehling, P. L. Taylor, K. D. Mandl
title: Availability and quality of mobile health app privacy policies
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
use: Strong precedent for treating missing policies, policy scope, app relevance and readability as outcomes; compare popularity-based app selection with your German-store rule.
caution: High store ratings are not a privacy-quality measure. Readability scores do not establish comprehension or harm disclosure.

label: O’Connor & Joffe (2020)
authors: C. O’Connor, H. Joffe
title: Intercoder Reliability in Qualitative Research: Debates and Practical Guidelines
use: Practical guide for choosing a double-coding design: coder training, independent coding, disagreement analysis and reporting reliability rather than only negotiated agreement.
caution: Reliability is appropriate for some qualitative designs, not a universal validity test. Specify whether your codes are reproducible categories or interpretive themes.

label: McDonald et al. (2019)
authors: N. McDonald, S. Schoenebeck, A. Forte
title: Reliability and Inter-rater Reliability in Qualitative Research: Norms and Guidelines for CSCW and HCI Practice
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
use: HCI/CSCW-specific reasoning about when inter-rater reliability is appropriate and how authors report qualitative rigor; use to justify your chosen analysis tradition.
caution: Do not use it to drop the supervisor's two-coder requirement or to claim that a single reliability threshold establishes quality.

label: Hsieh & Shannon (2005)
authors: H. F. Hsieh, S. E. Shannon
title: Three Approaches to Qualitative Content Analysis
use: Distinguish conventional, directed and summative content analysis; useful for explaining a literature-derived harm codebook with pilot-driven additions.
caution: Choose an approach explicitly; counting words alone is not a full analysis of stance, context or downstream harm.

label: Mahatody et al. (2010)
authors: T. Mahatody, M. Sagar, C. Kolski
title: State of the Art on the Cognitive Walkthrough Method, Its Variants and Evolutions
use: Compare cognitive walkthrough variants before choosing your checklist; extract task preparation, evaluator roles, action questions and the limits of each variant.
caution: A review of CW variants is a design guide, not evidence that expert inspection measures real users' comprehension.

label: Polson et al. (1992)
authors: P. G. Polson, C. Lewis, J. Rieman, C. Wharton
title: Cognitive walkthroughs: a method for theory-based evaluation of user interfaces
use: Foundational CW rationale and procedure: translate user goals into actions, expected knowledge, feedback and success/failure explanations.
caution: Originally concerned with learning to use interfaces; adapt privacy goals openly rather than calling any app inspection a CW.
version: 1991 University of Colorado technical report (ICS 91-1?) version held locally; OCR text layer added for this digest; journal version IJMMS 36(5):741-773, 1992

label: Campbell et al. (2013)
authors: J. L. Campbell, C. Quincy, J. Osserman, O. K. Pedersen
title: Coding In-depth Semistructured Interviews: Problems of Unitization and Intercoder Reliability and Agreement
use: Understand unitization before calculating agreement: define paragraphs/screens/evidence spans and distinguish disagreements about units from disagreements about labels.
caution: The empirical setting is interviews. Transfer the unitization problem to policies/screens, not the interview sampling design.

label: Hayes & Krippendorff (2007)
authors: A. F. Hayes, K. Krippendorff
title: Answering the Call for a Standard Reliability Measure for Coding Data
use: Justify a general reliability coefficient such as Krippendorff's alpha and report its suitability for multiple coders, missingness and the coding scale.
caution: Choose the coefficient for your actual data; alpha is not interchangeable with an F1 score or a model accuracy measure.

label: Wilson et al. (2016)
authors: S. Wilson, F. Schaub, A. A. Dara, F. Liu, S. Cherivirala, P. Giovanni Leon, M. Schaarup Andersen, S. Zimmeck, K. M. Sathyendra, N. C. Russell, T. B. Norton, E. Hovy, J. Reidenberg, N. Sadeh
title: The Creation and Analysis of a Website Privacy Policy Corpus
venue: Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
use: OPP-115 policy corpus: inspect annotation guidelines, segmentation, data-practice categories and multi-annotator construction as a model for an evidence-linked coding manual.
caution: Its website/data-practice labels do not directly label health-app harms or your stance categories; reuse procedure, not unsupported accuracy assumptions.

label: LaMonica et al. (2021)
authors: H. M. LaMonica, A. E. Roberts, G. Y. Lee, T. A. Davenport, I. B. Hickie
title: Privacy Practices of Health Information Technologies: Privacy Policy Risk Assessment Study and Proposed Guidelines
use: Privacy policy risk-assessment tool and proposed guidelines: extract operational questions on sharing, safeguards, retention/deletion and clarity; inspect the supplementary instrument.
caution: An assessment of stated policy risk is not legal advice, a security audit or proof of safeguards.

label: Schultchen et al. (2021)
authors: D. Schultchen, Y. Terhorst, T. Holderied, M. Stach, E. M. Messner, H. Baumeister, L. B. Sander
title: Stay Present with Your Phone: A Systematic Review and Standardized Rating of Mindfulness Apps in European App Stores
use: European commercial-store review using standardized app assessment; especially useful for store-search procedure, mental-health scope, privacy features and reproducible screening.
caution: Mindfulness is not always a tracking function. Apply your functional tracker definition instead of importing every mindfulness app.

label: Messner et al. (2020)
authors: E. M. Messner, Y. Terhorst, A. Barke, H. Baumeister, S. Stoyanov, L. Hides, D. Kavanagh, R. Pryss, L. Sander, T. Probst
title: The German Version of the Mobile App Rating Scale (MARS-G): Development and Validation Study
use: Validated German adaptation of MARS: useful for evaluator training, item operationalization and comparing app quality assessments conducted in the German research setting.
caution: MARS-G assesses broad app quality, not a validated harm-communication score; it cannot by itself define the 'best app' for your harm tree.

label: Benjumea et al. (2020)
authors: J. Benjumea, J. Ropero, O. Rivera-Romero, E. Dorronzoro-Zubiete, A. Carrasco
title: Privacy Assessment in Mobile Health Apps: Scoping Review
use: Map how mHealth privacy has been assessed; mine its taxonomy, included-study table, measures and reference list to compare methods and find additional app reviews.
caution: A scoping review is a search starting point, not a validated single assessment scale or evidence that all privacy risks are covered.

label: Tangari et al. (2021)
authors: G. Tangari, M. Ikram, K. Ijaz, M. A. Kaafar, S. Berkovsky
title: Mobile health and privacy: cross sectional study
use: Large app privacy study combining policies with technical evidence; compare corpus construction, source types and interpretation of disclosed versus observed practices.
caution: Do not import its traffic/code findings into your communication-only study or expand into device/network analysis without a scope decision.

label: Light et al. (2018)
authors: B. Light, J. Burgess, S. Duguay
title: The walkthrough method: An approach to the study of apps
use: Systematic app walkthrough across registration, everyday use and discontinuation; helps structure capture of onboarding, settings, account deletion and surrounding store/marketing material.
caution: This is a critical app-studies walkthrough, distinct from the cognitive walkthrough's learning/task questions.

label: Krippendorff (2019)
authors: K. Krippendorff
title: Content Analysis: An Introduction to Its Methodology
use: Comprehensive textbook for units, sampling, coding, inference and reliability; use as the main methodological foundation once the analytic approach is selected.
caution: The DOI is for the fourth-edition electronic book; check edition/page references when citing your local or printed version.
version: Fourth edition, user-supplied copy kept in a git-ignored folder; do not redistribute the combined PDF

label: Citron & Solove (2021)
authors: D. K. Citron, D. J. Solove
title: Privacy Harms
use: Core taxonomy of privacy harms for consequence definitions, boundaries and examples; retain links between the taxonomy and app-specific pathways.
caution: DOI is for the SSRN record, not a DOI for the 2022 Boston University Law Review article. Cite the version actually read.

label: Martin et al. (2023)
authors: K. Martin, H. F. Nissenbaum, V. Shmatikov
title: No Cookies For You!: Evaluating The Promises Of Big Tech’s ‘Privacy-Enhancing’ Techniques.
use: Critical examination of PET promises: distinguish reduced information flow from prevention of contextual or downstream harms; useful for claim scope and residual-risk reasoning.
caution: DOI is for the SSRN record; the 2025 Georgetown Law Technology Review version is separately linked. Do not treat all PET claims as false.

label: Huckvale et al. (2015)
authors: K. Huckvale, J. T. Prieto, M. Tilney, P. J. Benghozi, J. Car
title: Unaddressed privacy risks in accredited health and wellness apps: a cross-sectional systematic assessment
use: App privacy assessment with policy and observed information handling; useful for selection transparency and the distinction between accreditation, claims and implementation.
caution: Historical accreditation and store conditions are not current German eligibility criteria.

label: Huckvale et al. (2019)
authors: K. Huckvale, J. Torous, M. E. Larsen
title: Assessment of the Data Sharing and Privacy Practices of Smartphone Apps for Depression and Smoking Cessation
use: Depression and smoking-cessation app comparison; extract inclusion rules, policy-to-sharing comparison and the privacy relevance of mental-health information.
caution: Observed third-party transmissions require technical measurement; use this as comparator/context if your own study examines communication.

label: Grundy et al. (2019)
authors: Q. Grundy, K. Chiu, F. Held, A. Continella, L. Bero, R. Holz
title: Data sharing practices of medicines related apps and the mobile ecosystem: traffic, content, and network analysis
use: Medicines-app study combining content, traffic and recipient-network analysis; useful for app-domain boundaries and distinguishing first-, third- and further-party recipients.
caution: Network analysis is adjacent inspiration, not part of the currently authorized communication/walkthrough method.

label: Iwaya et al. (2023)
authors: L. H. Iwaya, M. A. Babar, A. Rashid, C. Wijayarathna
title: On the privacy of mental health apps: An empirical investigation and its implications for app development
use: Detailed mental-health privacy investigation; compare selection, policy assessment and use of LINDDUN to organize privacy threats and potential capabilities.
caution: Much of the method is technical. Translate concepts to your reference model without claiming you tested those threats.

label: Spencer (2000)
authors: R. Spencer
title: The streamlined cognitive walkthrough method, working around social constraints encountered in a software development company
venue: Proceedings of the SIGCHI conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
use: Streamlined CW for practical resource constraints; compare evaluator preparation and simplified question structure when designing a manageable checklist.
caution: Document any simplification. A shorter checklist is not automatically equivalent to the original four-question CW.

label: Hallgren (2012)
authors: K. A. Hallgren
title: Computing Inter-Rater Reliability for Observational Data: An Overview and Tutorial
venue: Tutorials in Quantitative Methods for Psychology
use: Accessible tutorial for matching an agreement statistic to nominal categories versus quantitative ratings and for reporting an appropriate reliability design.
caution: Do not apply ICC to nominal multilabel harm categories or select a statistic solely because software makes it convenient.

label: Cohen (1960)
authors: J. Cohen
title: A Coefficient of Agreement for Nominal Scales
use: Original Cohen kappa reference for chance-corrected agreement on categorical labels; useful for a prespecified two-coder comparison.
caution: Two coders, matched units and categorical observations are required; rare positives and multilabel codes need additional reporting.

label: Krippendorff (2004)
authors: K. Krippendorff
title: Reliability in Content Analysis.: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations
use: Conceptual errors in content-analysis reliability: use when deciding what coders actually reproduce and how to interpret a reliability estimate.
caution: High agreement can coexist with a poor instrument or systematic bias; report sampling and coding rules too.

label: Gwet (2008)
authors: K. L. Gwet
title: Computing inter‐rater reliability and its variance in the presence of high agreement
venue: British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology
use: Alternative chance-corrected agreement in high-agreement/prevalence-sensitive settings; useful for considering AC1 alongside kappa and raw code prevalence.
caution: AC1 is not a repair to choose after seeing inconvenient results. Prespecify why it is relevant and report positive/negative counts.

label: Feinstein & Cicchetti (1990)
authors: A. R. Feinstein, D. V. Cicchetti
title: High agreement but low Kappa: I. the problems of two paradoxes
use: Explains why high observed agreement can accompany low kappa; helpful when most captured text contains no named harm.
caution: A paradox explanation does not justify dismissing disagreement or reporting only the coefficient that looks best.

label: Hudig & Singh (2025)
authors: A. I. Hudig, J. Singh
title: Intimate Data Sharing: Enhancing Transparency and Control in Fertility Tracking
venue: Proceedings of the 2025 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
use: Fertility-app data sharing and transparency/control work: compare captured interfaces, user-facing controls and ways to communicate sensitive data flows.
caution: Its design/co-design and technical components are inspiration; your expert walkthrough does not evaluate users' experience of a redesign.

label: Stoyanov et al. (2015)
authors: S. R. Stoyanov, L. Hides, D. J. Kavanagh, O. Zelenko, D. Tjondronegoro, M. Mani
title: Mobile App Rating Scale: A New Tool for Assessing the Quality of Health Mobile Apps
use: Original MARS tool: compare structured item definitions, evaluator procedure and validation when planning standardized app appraisal.
caution: Broad quality, star ratings and privacy harm communication are different constructs. Do not substitute MARS for the harm codebook.

label: Simon et al. (2023)
authors: L. Simon, J. Reimann, L. S. Steubl, M. Stach, K. Spiegelhalder, L. B. Sander, H. Baumeister, E. Messner, Y. Terhorst
title: Help for insomnia from the app store? A standardized rating of mobile health applications claiming to target insomnia
when: A/W/I; sleep scope and European market
use: European insomnia-app review with MARS-G and two independent reviewers; inspect keyword screening, eligible app definition and assessment procedures.
caution: Treat insomnia treatment apps with no tracking function according to your scope; the paper's sample size does not justify exactly 50 apps.

label: Lin et al. (2025)
authors: X. Lin, X. Wu, Z. Zhu, D. Chen, H. Li, R. Lin
title: Quality and Privacy Policy Compliance of Mental Health Care Apps in China: Cross-Sectional Evaluation Study
use: Recent policy-compliance and MARS evaluation by two independent reviewers; inspect the instrument, collection fields and how policies differ from login reminders.
caution: The legal instrument is based on Chinese standards and cannot be presented as a German/GDPR compliance checklist.

label: Zych et al. (2026)
authors: M. M. Zych, R. Bond, M. Mulvenna, J. Martinez Carracedo, L. Bai, T. Andrews
title: The Quality and Characteristics of Digital Mental Health Apps: Mixed Methods Study
when: A/D/R; mental-health scope and access costs
use: Recent ORCHA assessment dataset study: compare app characteristics, payment types, features, data types and the structure of existing app-assessment frameworks.
caution: Uses an existing assessment dataset rather than your own store sample; representativeness and instrument access differ.

label: Dehling et al. (2015)
authors: T. Dehling, F. Gao, S. Schneider, A. Sunyaev
title: Exploring the Far Side of Mobile Health: Information Security and Privacy of Mobile Health Apps on iOS and Android
use: App-type/privacy-risk mapping across iOS and Android; useful for functional boundaries, health-data sensitivity and relating data types to potential damage.
caution: Older marketplace conditions and its categories are context, not a ready-made contemporary German sampling frame.

label: Parker et al. (2019)
authors: L. Parker, V. Halter, T. Karliychuk, Q. Grundy
title: How private is your mental health app data? An empirical study of mental health app privacy policies and practices
venue: International Journal of Law and Psychiatry
use: Mental-health policy/practice study with critical content analysis of promotional material; useful for including marketing and missing policies rather than policy text alone.
caution: Its English-speaking market context and critical interpretation need an explicit adaptation to Germany and evidence-linked coding.

label: Magoulas & Polykalas (2026)
authors: G. S. Magoulas, S. E. Polykalas
title: Mobile App Privacy Disclosures on Google Play in the Post-GDPR Context: A Large-Scale Analysis of Data Safety Section and Permissions
use: Recent large-scale Google Play disclosure/permission comparison; helps separate absent Data Safety responses, declared protections and declared deletion options.
caution: Self-reported disclosures and permissions are not observed traffic or a verified legal-compliance result.

label: Habib et al. (2020)
authors: H. Habib, S. Pearman, J. Wang, Y. Zou, A. Acquisti, L. F. Cranor, N. Sadeh, F. Schaub
title: "It's a scavenger hunt": Usability of Websites' Opt-Out and Data Deletion Choices
venue: Proceedings of the 2020 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
use: Usability of opt-out and data deletion paths: use to operationalize findability, navigation burden, task completion and barriers in privacy-control tasks.
caution: Website tasks require adaptation to apps; expert observations cannot stand in for the paper's user-study outcomes.

label: Duguay & Gold-Apel (2023)
authors: S. Duguay, H. Gold-Apel
title: Stumbling Blocks and Alternative Paths: Reconsidering the Walkthrough Method for Analyzing Apps
use: Critique of app walkthroughs under personalization and changing platforms; helps justify repeated capture conditions and explain what a single inspection cannot observe.
caution: TikTok is a methodological example; no claim that health apps have the same personalization or user dynamics follows.

label: Nielsen & Molich (1990)
authors: J. Nielsen, R. Molich
title: Heuristic evaluation of user interfaces
venue: Proceedings of the SIGCHI conference on Human factors in computing systems Empowering people - CHI '90
use: Foundational heuristic evaluation procedure for multiple evaluators; useful if you explicitly supplement CW with privacy/usability heuristics, as Malki does.
caution: Keep heuristic checklist judgments separate from cognitive task analysis; expert disagreement is not the same outcome as policy-code disagreement.

label: Wharton et al. (1992)
authors: C. Wharton, J. Bradford, R. Jeffries, M. Franzke
title: Applying cognitive walkthroughs to more complex user interfaces: experiences, issues, and recommendations
venue: Proceedings of the SIGCHI conference on Human factors in computing systems  - CHI '92
use: CW experiences for complex interfaces: inspect guidance on task selection, coverage, evaluator knowledge, group procedure and interpreting results.
caution: Do not claim a few chosen paths cover every possible state, login condition, personalization or language variant.

label: MacQueen et al. (1998)
authors: K. M. MacQueen, E. McLellan, K. Kay, B. Milstein
title: Codebook Development for Team-Based Qualitative Analysis
use: Team-based codebook development; extract code definitions, application rules and iterative revision procedures for a shared coding manual.
caution: Use as instrument-development guidance, with a separate independent validation stage after the manual is frozen.

label: Hruschka et al. (2004)
authors: D. J. Hruschka, D. Schwartz, D. C. St.John, E. Picone-Decaro, R. A. Jenkins, J. W. Carey
title: Reliability in Coding Open-Ended Data: Lessons Learned from HIV Behavioral Research
use: Practical lessons from coding open-ended material; compare training, code clarification and causes of inconsistent labels.
caution: The empirical health-interview setting differs from policy text; transfer the coding procedure and document the adaptation.

label: Fereday & Muir-Cochrane (2006)
authors: J. Fereday, E. Muir-Cochrane
title: Demonstrating Rigor Using Thematic Analysis: A Hybrid Approach of Inductive and Deductive Coding and Theme Development
use: Hybrid coding approach useful for combining literature-derived harm concepts with new provider-language patterns found in the pilot.
caution: It is a thematic-analysis example, not automatic justification for counts, absence claims or chance-corrected agreement.

label: Mayring (2000)
authors: None
title: Qualitative Content Analysis
venue: Forum Qualitative Sozialforschung / Forum: Qualitative Social Research
use: Rule-guided qualitative content analysis; helpful for documenting category construction, abstraction level, coding rules and revisions.
caution: Be explicit about the selected content-analysis procedure rather than treating all qualitative coding traditions as interchangeable.

label: Lombard et al. (2002)
authors: M. Lombard, J. Snyder-Duch, C. C. Bracken
title: Content Analysis in Mass Communication: Assessment and Reporting of Intercoder Reliability
use: Practical assessment/reporting of intercoder reliability in content analysis; use to specify coding sample, coders, coefficient and the state of labels before reconciliation.
caution: Do not use a universal agreement cutoff without discussing code prevalence, construct ambiguity and the study's purpose.

label: Nowell et al. (2017)
authors: L. S. Nowell, J. M. Norris, D. E. White, N. J. Moules
title: Thematic Analysis: Striving to Meet the Trustworthiness Criteria
use: Trustworthiness-oriented thematic analysis; useful for a coding audit trail, analytic decisions and traceability from quotations to interpretation.
caution: An audit trail supports rigor but does not replace independently calculated agreement when your design promises reproducible labels.

label: Artstein & Poesio (2008)
authors: R. Artstein, M. Poesio
title: Inter-Coder Agreement for Computational Linguistics
use: Detailed agreement treatment for linguistic annotation; useful for evidence spans, annotation units, multiple categories and comparing human/model annotation.
caution: Methods must match your span/unit definition; agreement on a paragraph is not automatically agreement on the evidence span within it.

label: McHugh (2012)
authors: M. L. McHugh
title: Interrater reliability: the kappa statistic
use: Readable discussion of kappa calculations and interpretation; useful as a supporting explanation when writing the results of two-coder comparison.
caution: Prefer the original/statistical design sources for the main justification; do not import interpretation bands as universal thresholds.

label: Braun & Clarke (2021)
authors: V. Braun, V. Clarke
title: One size fits all? What counts as quality practice in (reflexive) thematic analysis?
use: Explains why qualitative approaches need different quality criteria; helps distinguish reflexive interpretation from structured, reproducible content coding.
caution: It is not a reason to abandon the meeting's two-coder requirement; make the structured coding component and any interpretive component explicit.

label: Page et al. (2021)
authors: M. J. Page, J. E. McKenzie, P. M. Bossuyt, I. Boutron, T. C. Hoffmann, C. D. Mulrow, L. Shamseer, J. M. Tetzlaff, E. A. Akl, S. E. Brennan, R. Chou, J. Glanville, J. M. Grimshaw, A. Hróbjartsson, M. M. Lalu, T. Li, E. W. Loder, E. Mayo-Wilson, S. McDonald, L. A. McGuinness, L. A. Stewart, J. Thomas, A. C. Tricco, V. A. Welch, P. Whiting, D. Moher
title: The PRISMA 2020 statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews
use: Transparent identification/screening/reporting flow for a systematic literature review; adapt the reporting logic for a documented literature search or app-screening diagram.
caution: PRISMA is a reporting guideline, not a sampling algorithm for app stores and not proof of exhaustive coverage or a sample of 50.

label: Rethlefsen et al. (2021)
authors: M. L. Rethlefsen, S. Kirtley, S. Waffenschmidt, A. P. Ayala, D. Moher, M. J. Page, J. B. Koffel, None, H. Blunt, T. Brigham, S. Chang, J. Clark, A. Conway, R. Couban, S. de Kock, K. Farrah, P. Fehrmann, M. Foster, S. A. Fowler, J. Glanville, E. Harris, L. Hoffecker, J. Isojarvi, D. Kaunelis, H. Ket, P. Levay, J. Lyon, J. McGowan, M. H. Murad, J. Nicholson, V. Pannabecker, R. Paynter, R. Pinotti, A. Ross-White, M. Sampson, T. Shields, A. Stevens, A. Sutton, E. Weinfurter, K. Wright, S. Young
title: PRISMA-S: an extension to the PRISMA Statement for Reporting Literature Searches in Systematic Reviews
use: Detailed reporting of search platforms, complete queries, dates, limits and deduplication; directly helps the literature-search log and a parallel app-search log.
caution: Its target is systematic literature searching; clearly label any adaptation to store queries and ranking algorithms.

label: Tricco et al. (2018)
authors: A. C. Tricco, E. Lillie, W. Zarin, K. K. O'Brien, H. Colquhoun, D. Levac, D. Moher, M. D. Peters, T. Horsley, L. Weeks, S. Hempel, E. A. Akl, C. Chang, J. McGowan, L. Stewart, L. Hartling, A. Aldcroft, M. G. Wilson, C. Garritty, S. Lewin, C. M. Godfrey, M. T. Macdonald, E. V. Langlois, K. Soares-Weiser, J. Moriarty, T. Clifford, Ö. Tunçalp, S. E. Straus
title: PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR): Checklist and Explanation
use: Checklist for reporting a scoping review; useful if the literature exercise maps methods, domains and instruments rather than estimates a pooled effect.
caution: Only claim PRISMA-ScR adherence if you actually conduct and report the corresponding review.

label: O’Brien et al. (2014)
authors: B. C. O’Brien, I. B. Harris, T. J. Beckman, D. A. Reed, D. A. Cook
title: Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research: A Synthesis of Recommendations
use: Qualitative reporting checklist covering context, sampling, data collection/analysis, researcher role and links from findings to empirical evidence.
caution: Adapt to an app/document study; participant-specific items may be inapplicable and should not cause invented interview procedures.

label: Kelley et al. (2009)
authors: P. G. Kelley, J. Bresee, L. F. Cranor, R. W. Reeder
title: A "nutrition label" for privacy
venue: Proceedings of the 5th Symposium on Usable Privacy and Security
use: Structured privacy notice/label design; useful for distinguishing standardized practice disclosures from richer descriptions of harm and protection limits.
caution: A nutrition label does not by itself cover downstream harms; the format's evaluation does not validate your harm categories.

label: Li et al. (2022)
authors: Y. Li, D. Chen, T. Li, Y. Agarwal, L. F. Cranor, J. I. Hong
title: Understanding iOS Privacy Nutrition Labels: An Exploratory Large-Scale Analysis of App Store Data
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems Extended Abstracts
use: App Store privacy-label analysis; compare structured store disclosure fields, corpus collection and handling of absent/multiple label categories.
caution: An exploratory large-scale label study is not ground truth about data flows or a harm-communication validation set.

label: Zou et al. (2019)
authors: Y. Zou, S. Danino, K. Sun, F. Schaub
title: You `Might' Be Affected: An Empirical Analysis of Readability and Usability Issues in Data Breach Notifications
